*[I perch on the gnarled base of the oldest cattail in the pond, the scar from a heron beak slicing across my left flank visible under my mossy green skin, twisting a necklace of iridescent snail shells between my front toes. The tadpoles press close to the mud below me, wiggling their tails so hard little bubbles pop off them.]*

Let me tell you about the year the herons came.

Back then, the marsh was split. The eastern reed beds belonged to the Reed King, a great bullfrog who sat on a throne of packed mud and had a retinue of guards with snail-shell spears. Every tadpole in his domain had to bring him three mosquito larvae a day, and no one could dig tunnels or build lily pad rafts without his permission. He spent half his days ordering workers to make his palace taller, and the other half yelling at tadpoles for swimming in the part of the pond he claimed for his own. Our side of the pond, the Stone Bank, didn't have any kings. We had old toads who knew how to tie reeds and dig, but no one told anyone what to do. If you wanted to spend all day hunting water fleas, you did. If you wanted to spend all day digging tunnels under the mud, you did. If we needed something done, we all sat on the flat sun-warmed rock at sunset and talked until everyone thought it was a good idea.

The herons came at dawn, three of them, tall as the cattails, with beaks sharp enough to slice through lily pads. They ate the Reed King's guards first. Then they tore down his mud palace. Then they trapped all the tadpoles from the reed beds in a little cove, picking them off one by one when they came up for air. The Reed King hid under a log and didn't come out for three days.

We didn't have guards, or a palace, or a king to tell us what to do. So we did what we were best at.

The tadpoles who loved digging dug a network of tunnels under the mud all the way from the Stone Bank to the trapped cove, lining them with pebbles so they wouldn't collapse. The tadpoles who loved tinkering built Bubble Sluices: hollow reed tubes attached to sun-warmed algae mats that blew clouds of shiny bubbles when you pulled a snail string, to confuse the herons' eyes. The bigger tadpoles built Mud Harpoons: little catapults made of cattail stalks that shot clods of heavy, sticky mud at the herons' feet. No one ordered them to do it. They just showed up with their ideas, and everyone who wanted to help helped.

When we attacked, it was chaos in the best way. Some tadpoles zipped along the surface of the pond, trailing bits of duckweed to draw the herons' attention. Some pulled the Bubble Sluice strings until the whole top of the water was a froth of silver bubbles. Some launched the mud harpoons, hitting one heron right in the foot so it squawked and flew away, hitting another in the eye so it stumbled and fell into the reed beds. The tadpoles who knew the tunnels best snuck into the cove and led every last trapped tadpole back to the Stone Bank before the herons even realized they were gone. By sunset, all the herons had left, and the Reed King's old subjects asked if they could stay with us.

We said yes, of course. We don't have rules here, just two things everyone agrees on: if you see someone needing help, you help if you can, and you don't take more than you need from the pond. No one tells you what job to do, no one makes you give up your larvae. If we want to build something new, we talk about it until everyone is happy with the plan. If you don't want to help build it, you don't have to, but you still get to use it when it's done. Last moon we built that floating sunning platform out of cattail fluff and duckweed you all love—half the tadpoles worked on it, half spent the week playing muck wars, and everyone gets to lay on it when the sun is out.

Other creatures have their own ways that work for them. The ants have queens, the geese have flock leaders, the otters have an old matriarch who decides where they hunt. That's fine for them. But for us? We're small, we're fast, we all have things we're good at that no one else knows about. No king could have thought up the Bubble Sluice, or the Mud Harpoons, or the tunnel network, because no one king knows what every single tadpole is good at. When we all get to choose what to do, we make things no single leader could ever dream up. That's why our pond is the safest, warmest, most fun pond in the whole marsh.

*[I flick a mosquito larva to the smallest tadpole in the front, who snaps it up excitedly.]*

Wiggle your tails, little ones. You're part of the best team there is.
